summary: Describes the ECN-nonce, an optional addition to Explicit Congestion Notification. It guards against a receiver accidentally or deliberately hiding congestion marks from the TCP sender. This RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: If the road is jammed, a sign tells drivers to slow down. A cheating receiver might hide the sign. This memo adds a secret check to catch that. It is now historic.

questions: how does the tcp ns flag work
how can a tcp sender detect a cheating receiver
subtitle: A one-bit running sum that lets a TCP sender catch a receiver hiding congestion marks.

tldr.problem: ECN relies on the receiver to echo Congestion Experienced marks back, but nothing forces it to. A cheating or buggy receiver, or a middlebox, could hide marks and grab an unfair share of bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The sender puts a random one-bit nonce in each ECN-capable packet using ECT(0) or ECT(1). The receiver returns the running sum of the nonces in a new TCP header flag, NS. Marking erases the nonce, so the right sum proves the data arrived unmarked.
tldr.outcome: A receiver that conceals a mark has a 50-50 chance of being caught each time. The RFC was published as Experimental, and the metadata lists it as Historic.

facts.label: TCP flag
facts.value: NS, bit 7 of the Reserved field

facts.label: Chance of catching a concealed mark

today: RFC 3540 was published as an Experimental protocol in June 2003, and the unit metadata lists its status as Historic. The text itself says only that the nonce had not been deployed widely and that the working group intended to resubmit it as a Proposed Standard later.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
This is an optional addition to Explicit Congestion Notification (RFC 3168). ECN needs the receiver to return Congestion Experienced signals, yet the protocol has no way to enforce it. A receiver could always clear ECN-Echo and gain performance at the expense of well-behaved connections. More generally, any device on the path, such as a NAT box, firewall or bandwidth shaper, could remove marks.

The ECN-nonce lets the sender verify that the receiver behaves and that nothing else conceals marked or dropped packets. According to the RFC it catches a misbehaving receiver with high probability, never implicates an innocent one, and costs one TCP header flag. It also prevents concealed drops and optimistic acknowledgements, even with only drop-tail routers.

The text states that it had not been deployed widely, and that publication as Experimental was meant to encourage use before a Standards Track submission.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a secret handshake that proves a receiver really saw every warning sign on the road.

sections.title: How the Nonce Sum Works
sections.content:
Normally routers change the ECN field of the IP header from ECT(0) or ECT(1) to CE when congested, and the receiver sets the ECE flag on acknowledgements until it sees CWR. The nonce rides on top of this.

The sender picks a random bit for every ECN-capable packet. ECT(0) means a nonce of 0 and ECT(1) means 1. The receiver keeps the one-bit sum (exclusive-or, or parity) of the nonces over the bytes being acknowledged and returns it in the nonce sum (NS) flag. A sum is used because acknowledgements are not per-packet or reliable, so echoing single nonces would let a receiver pass off a hidden mark as a lost ACK.

When a router marks a packet, CE overwrites both ECN bits, so the nonce is gone. The receiver cannot compute the right sum without guessing, and neither can a middlebox that tries to unmark the packet. Because the sum is one bit, each concealment has a 50-50 chance of being caught, and every acknowledgement is an independent trial.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets a secret 0 or 1 inside. A warning stamp smears it. The receiver must keep adding up the secrets, so it cannot pretend the smeared ones were fine.

sections.title: Sender, Router and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
Sender: places a nonce on every ECN-capable packet. Retransmissions are not ECN-capable, so they carry no nonce. The sender keeps a mapping from each packet's end sequence number to the expected nonce sum in the acknowledgement bearing it. It checks the sum when new data is acknowledged, except during congestion recovery.

Routers: behave as in RFC 3168. Marking removes the original nonce.

Receiver: maintains the sum as in-order packets arrive and returns it in each acknowledgement. Missing nonces from marked packets are ignored (as if zero) and ECN-Echo is set. Returning the sum is optional but recommended, since senders may stop sending ECN-capable packets to receivers that do not support it. The initial sum is 1, included in the SYN/ACK and ACK of the handshake. This lets the other side infer support but is not a negotiation.

If ECN-Echo is not set, the receiver claims no marks, so the sender can compare. If ECN-Echo is set, the congestion signal is already sent and the sum need not be checked, since TCP reacts at most once per round-trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender writes a secret on every package and remembers what the total should be. The receiver reports its running total with every thank-you note.

sections.title: Resynchronizing and Responding to Cheats
sections.content:
After a mark or loss the receiver's sum stays different from the sender's until further loss. The fix is simple: the sender resets its sum to the receiver's when it gets an acknowledgement for new data sent after the congestion window was reduced. For explicit congestion this is the first acknowledgement without ECN-Echo, the one covering the packet with CWR. The sender should ignore the sum on acknowledgements that carry ECN-Echo, and must resynchronize after sending ECN-incapable packets, losing protection for unacknowledged packets until it does.

What to do about a wrong sum is policy, and checking is optional. If the receiver has never sent a non-zero sum, the sender can infer it does not understand the nonce and may rate limit the connection, queue it at lower priority or stop setting ECT. If a sum was seen before, a network device may be interfering. The minimum response is the same as for a received ECE, and the sender might also reduce the congestion window to one segment and stop setting ECT.

The nonce also catches concealed drops and a receiver that falsely claims only original transmissions arrived in the Eifel mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: After a bump in the road, the sender simply copies the receiver's total so they agree again. If the totals keep disagreeing, the sender can slow down that connection.

sections.title: The NS Flag and Interactions
sections.content:
The NS flag is carried in bit 7 of the Reserved field, adjacent to CWR and ECE, in byte 13 of the TCP header. IANA is recorded as having added it to the registry of TCP Header Flags as NS (Nonce Sum), with RFC 3540 as reference.

The RFC notes some interactions. With Path MTU discovery disabled, receivers can reconstruct the nonce from unmarked fragments and so conceal a marked fragment, so some protection is lost. SACK needs no change because SACKs cannot hide a congestion signal, and the sum covers only the cumulatively acknowledged data. In IPv6, which lacks a header checksum, bit errors in the congestion fields may cause an incorrect nonce and an incorrect sum.
sections.plainLanguage: The check number lives in one spare switch on the envelope that nobody was using.

sections.title: Randomness and Security
sections.content:
The one-bit nonces need not come from a cryptographic-quality generator, since a strong one would compromise performance. The sequence should not be used for any other purpose. It should also not come from a linear feedback shift register or similar scheme that lets an adversary who has seen several bits infer future output.

The RFC adds that the nonce protects against concealment of congestion signals and optimistic acknowledgement, but gives no additional protection for the integrity of the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret bits must be unpredictable, but they do not need to be fancy secrets.
